title: Parametric Polymorphism
body:
> **Two different things share the word "polymorphism"**, and this course means the one Introduction to Software Engineering does not. [[Polymorphism]] owns the object-oriented sense: one interface,
> many implementations, chosen at run time by the object's actual type. This note owns the
> parametric sense: **one** implementation that works for every type, erased before run time.
> Neither is a special case of the other. They are different mechanisms answering different
> questions, and the shared name is a historical accident.

```haskell
length  :: [a] -> Int
reverse :: [a] -> [a]
fst     :: (a, b) -> a
```

The `a` is a **type variable**, universally quantified: these signatures promise to work for
every choice of `a`. And there is exactly one body of code. `length` counts cells and never
looks at an element, `reverse` rearranges pointers, `fst` projects a field. None of them can
inspect the values, because none of them know anything about `a`.

That last sentence is the whole idea. **Knowing nothing about the type is the source of the
guarantee, not a limitation.**

## The two senses side by side

| | Parametric (this course) | Subtype / OO ([[Polymorphism]]) |
|---|---|---|
| Question answered | one algorithm, any element type | one call site, many behaviours |
| Number of implementations | **one** | one per subclass |
| What varies | the type it is instantiated at | the code that runs |
| Chosen | at compile time | at run time, by the object |
| Requires | nothing of the type | a common [[Interface]] or superclass |
| Mechanism | type variables | a vtable and [[Overriding\|overriding]] |
| Cost | none at run time | an indirect call |
| In [[Java]] | generics, `List<T>` | `Shape s = new Circle()` |
| Failure mode | none; it cannot inspect the value | forgetting `@Override`, or an `instanceof` chain |

[[Java]] has both and the row that shows it clearly is the last two: `List<T>` is parametric,
`s.draw()` is subtype. Java's generics are erased at compile time, so `List<String>` and
`List<Integer>` are the same class at run time, which is precisely the parametric story. C++
templates are a third answer again, generating a separate copy per instantiation.

[[C]] has neither, which is why `qsort` takes a `void *` and a comparison function pointer and
throws away all type safety to get one implementation. That is the problem parametric
polymorphism solves, and the `void *` is the shape of the hole.

## Parametricity: the free theorem

The reason this is more than convenience. Because a parametric function cannot inspect its
values, **the type alone constrains what the function can do**:

| Signature | Possible implementations |
|---|---|
| `a -> a` | exactly one: the identity |
| `a -> b -> a` | exactly one: return the first |
| `[a] -> [a]` | many, but every one only rearranges, duplicates, or drops elements; none can invent an `a` or examine one |
| `[a] -> Int` | must compute from the *length* alone; the elements are unreachable |

So `reverse :: [a] -> [a]` cannot possibly sort, cannot special-case integers, and cannot
depend on the contents. You know that from the signature without reading the code, and the
formal version of this is called a **free theorem**. Nothing similar is available in the OO
sense, where the whole point is that the implementation varies invisibly.

This is also why [[Static Typing]] claims signatures are documentation, and why a well-chosen
signature narrows a function to nearly one implementation.

## When you do need to know something about the type

Parametric polymorphism's guarantee comes from knowing nothing, so a function that must compare
or print its elements cannot be purely parametric. That is what [[Type Class]] constraints are
for, and it is the third kind of polymorphism:

```haskell
sort :: Ord a => [a] -> [a]     -- parametric in a, but a must be orderable
```

Read the constraint as the exact amount of knowledge being bought back. `sort` still has one
implementation for all types; it just requires the type to supply a comparison.

## Core Facts to Know

- **Not the OO sense**; see [[Polymorphism]] for that one.
- Parametric: one implementation, universally quantified over a type variable.
- Subtype/OO: many implementations, one call site, dispatched at run time.
- A parametric function cannot inspect its values, which is where its guarantee comes from.
- **Parametricity**: the signature constrains the implementation. `a -> a` can only be `id`.
- These consequences are called **free theorems**; you get them without reading the code.
- Java generics are parametric and erased; `Shape s = new Circle()` is subtype dispatch.
- C's `void *` plus a function pointer is the untyped version of the same need.
- A [[Type Class]] constraint (`Ord a =>`) buys back exactly the knowledge you need.
- Ad-hoc polymorphism ([[Type Class]]) is the third kind: different code per type.
